items.prompt: What did 'take care of it' fail to say in the vendor incident?
choices: How much authority the report had
Which CI tools the team already used
Whether the contract mattered to the team
items.explanation: The verb carried no level, so the report and the manager each guessed a different amount of authority.

items.prompt: Delegation is best described as:
choices: A choice between doing it yourself or dropping it
A one-time handoff after which you stop looking
A spectrum of how much autonomy the delegate has
items.explanation: Autonomy comes in degrees, from doing exactly what is said to acting alone, so delegation is a spectrum.

items.prompt: In the vendor incident, who was careless?
choices: The report, for skipping the approval step
Neither; the level was never spoken aloud
The manager, for choosing the wrong person
items.explanation: The level was never stated, so each person acted reasonably on a different assumption.

items.prompt: Which sentence actually names a level?
choices: Research options and bring me a recommendation first
Just handle the whole vendor thing for us sometime this month, please
Take care of it however you see fit, thanks
items.explanation: Only that sentence says what the delegate may do and what comes back to the manager.

items.prompt: Is the highest possible autonomy always the best delegation?
choices: Yes; giving more freedom always builds more trust in the person
Yes; any check-in only signals a lack of trust
No; it depends on the task and the delegate's context
items.explanation: More autonomy than the delegate's context supports invites avoidable mistakes, so higher is not automatically better.

items.prompt: What did the manager assume in the incident?
choices: Do exactly the steps I give you, with no deviation
Recommend a decision, then I approve it
Decide and act, then tell me afterward
items.explanation: The manager expected a recommendation and an approval step, which is Level 3.

items.prompt: In this unit, 'trust but verify' means:
choices: One light check-in at a key moment
A review of every step the delegate takes
A promise never to check in at all
items.explanation: Trust but verify is one chosen check-in, not review of everything and not no review.

items.prompt: When should a manager say the level out loud?
choices: Only after a mismatch has already happened
Once, at the start of a person's first week
Before delegating any non-trivial task
items.explanation: The level should be stated before the work starts, since the mismatch only shows up after it is too late to fix cheaply.

items.prompt: A manager says 'own the onboarding docs rewrite.' The report rewrites and publishes everything; the manager wanted a draft to review first. What is the best diagnosis?
choices: The report lacks judgment and should get less freedom going forward
The manager should have reviewed every page along the way
The level of authority was never named, so each assumed their own
The verb 'own' is too weak and should have been 'handle'
items.explanation: The mismatch was in the level, not the work. Naming it fixes the gap; lowering freedom or reviewing everything treats the wrong cause.
items.reference:
Said vs. meant
said: take care of picking a CI vendor
manager meant: recommend, I approve
report heard: decide and act
Why: a vague verb carries no level, so each person fills in their own.
items.learnMore:
Naming the level

Delegation is a spectrum of autonomy. The skill is saying where on it this task sits, out loud, instead of letting a verb like 'handle' imply it.

Common mistake

Assuming last time's level, or the obvious reading of the task, applies again.
items.reflection: Think of a time you handed off or received a task with a vague verb. What would the one sentence naming the level have been?

items.prompt: Which opening sentence best prevents the vendor mismatch?
choices: Research options and loop me in at finalists, before signing
Take care of the vendor and make sure it is a good fit for the team's budget
Handle it, and let me know if anything looks unusual
Own the vendor choice and keep the budget in mind
items.explanation: Only the first states what the delegate can decide and when the manager joins. The others are vague verbs.

items.prompt: Two reports get the same request. One asks 'do you want a recommendation or a decision?' and the other starts working. Why is the first approach stronger?
choices: It shows the report is unsure of their own ability and needs more guidance
It hands the real decision back to the manager
It saves time because the research can be skipped
It surfaces the level before any work depends on a guess
items.explanation: Asking turns a silent assumption into a stated level. It does not hand back the decision or skip the work.

items.prompt: A manager says 'I always give maximum autonomy; it is the most respectful way to delegate.' What is the strongest critique?
choices: Maximum autonomy is fine, but managers must still read every output before it is shared
Autonomy beyond the delegate's context sets them up for avoidable errors
Respect is shown through frequent status meetings instead
Delegation should always start at doing exactly what is said
items.explanation: Fit matters more than maximum. The other options either contradict the idea or swap it for a fixed policy.

items.prompt: What is Level 1 on the spectrum?
choices: Do exactly what I say
Decide and tell me afterward
Full autonomy, no report needed
items.explanation: Level 1 is the narrowest: the delegate follows instructions with no decisions of their own.

items.prompt: What is Level 3?
choices: Decide and act, then tell me after
Research options and I choose
Recommend a decision and I approve it
items.explanation: Level 3 has the delegate recommend while the manager keeps the final approval.

items.prompt: What is Level 5?
choices: Recommend and wait for my approval
Decide and act, then tell me after
Do exactly the steps I specified
items.explanation: Level 5 lets the delegate decide and act, informing the manager only after the fact.

items.prompt: Which levels were mismatched in the vendor incident?
choices: Level 3 on the manager's side, Level 5 on the report's
Level 1 on the manager's side, Level 2 on the report's
Level 4 on the manager's side, Level 6 on the report's
items.explanation: The manager was at Level 3 and the report acted at Level 5, a two-level gap.

items.prompt: How many named levels does the spectrum have?
choices: Two levels
Three levels
Six levels
items.explanation: The spectrum has six named stops from doing exactly what is said to full autonomy.

items.prompt: At Level 6, when is the manager involved?
choices: At every step of the work
Only if the delegate asks
Before each action is taken
items.explanation: Level 6 is full autonomy: the manager hears from the delegate only when the delegate chooses to say something.

items.prompt: At Level 2, what does the delegate decide?
choices: Which options are worth putting forward
The final decision, entirely alone
Nothing, since every step is dictated
items.explanation: At Level 2 the delegate gathers and filters options while the manager makes the decision.

items.prompt: Does a wide level gap always cause a failure?
choices: Yes; any gap eventually causes an incident
Yes, but only when it reaches Level 6
No; the cost of a wrong call matters too
items.explanation: A gap is a risk factor; whether it hurts depends on how costly and hard to reverse a wrong call is.

items.prompt: A manager says 'pick the caterer and tell me before you book.' Which level is that?
choices: Level 4: decide, but tell me before acting
Level 3: recommend a choice, and I approve it before booking
Level 5: decide and act, tell me after
Level 2: research options, and I decide
items.explanation: Telling before acting is Level 4. Level 3 needs approval; Level 5 informs only after.
items.reference:
The six levels
1 do exactly what I say
2-3 research, then recommend
4-5 decide, tell before or after
6 full autonomy
Why: each step up moves one more decision from the manager to the delegate.
items.learnMore:
A concrete spectrum

Six named stops let two people point at the same place instead of arguing over verbs. The incident was Level 3 on one side and Level 5 on the other.

Common mistake

Reading the numbers as a ranking of people instead of a description of one task.
items.reflection: Pick a task you currently hand off. Which of the six levels is it really at, and would the other person say the same number?

items.prompt: A report hears 'bring me your recommendation' but signs the contract. What went wrong?
choices: They acted at Level 1 on a Level 4 request
They skipped Level 2 and stopped at Level 3
They acted at Level 6 on a Level 2 request
They acted at Level 5 on a Level 3 request
items.explanation: Signing is deciding and acting. The request only authorized a recommendation, which is Level 3.

items.prompt: What separates Level 4 from Level 5?
choices: Whether the delegate is expected to do any research beforehand at all
Whether the manager hears before the action or after it
Whether the delegate is allowed to make decisions
Whether the manager reviews the final outcome
items.explanation: Both levels let the delegate decide. The difference is whether the manager can still object before the action.

choices: Contracts need a higher level than drafts by definition
Draft announcements never involve any delegation
A wrong contract call is costly and hard to reverse
The gap is smaller when the task is smaller
items.explanation: The gap is identical in both cases. What differs is the price and reversibility of a wrong call.

items.prompt: What is the first question for choosing a level?
choices: How reversible is a wrong call?
How long has the person worked here?
How busy is the manager this week?
items.explanation: Reversibility sets how expensive a wrong decision would be, which is the first thing to read.

items.prompt: What is the second question?
choices: How much it will cost to schedule the work this quarter?
How many people are watching the outcome?
How much relevant context does the delegate have?
items.explanation: Context is the delegate's own knowledge of this kind of decision, which is the second thing to read.

items.prompt: An easy-to-undo task leans toward:
choices: Lower levels, roughly 1 to 2, in all cases
Higher levels, roughly 4 to 6
Level 1 in every case
items.explanation: When a mistake is cheap to undo, there is little reason to hold back autonomy.

items.prompt: Hard to undo plus limited context points to:
choices: Levels 1 to 2
Levels 5 to 6
Level 6 only
items.explanation: Costly mistakes and thin context together call for the low levels, where the manager is involved early.

items.prompt: Can one person sit at different levels for different tasks?
choices: No; each person has one fixed level
Only after an annual review of the person
Yes; the level follows the task and context
items.explanation: The level follows the task and the context, so the same person can differ from task to task.

items.prompt: Which task is hardest to undo?
choices: Drafting a first announcement draft
Signing a one-year contract with a fee
Reordering a personal to-do list
items.explanation: A year-long contract with a fee is costly to reverse; a draft and a to-do list are cheap to change.

items.prompt: Why did the vendor task call for Level 2 or 3?
choices: It was hard to undo and the report's first time
The report was known to be rather unreliable on past work
The manager happened to be very busy
items.explanation: Both questions pointed down: the decision was costly to undo and new to the report.

items.prompt: Is the chosen level a personality trait of the delegate?
choices: Yes; it reflects how trustworthy they are at work
Yes; it is fixed at the time of hiring
No; it comes from two questions about the task
items.explanation: The level comes from reading the task and context, not from judging the person's character.

items.prompt: A report has run three similar evaluations well. The contract can be cancelled free within 30 days. Which level fits best?
choices: Level 1 or 2: new contracts always need close control
Level 3: every contract needs approval
Level 6: no report needed for proven people
Level 4 or 5: both questions favor autonomy
items.explanation: Easy to undo and strong context favor high autonomy. Level 6 skips even the report-back, which is more than needed.
items.reference:
Two questions
1 how reversible is a wrong call?
2 how much context does the delegate have?
hard to undo + little context: levels 1-2
Why: stakes and context together point to a level; neither alone decides it.
items.learnMore:
Choosing, not defaulting

A level is picked by reading the task: how costly a mistake would be, and how much the delegate already knows about this kind of decision.

Common mistake

Using one fixed level for everyone, or picking it from how much you like the person.
items.reflection: Take one task you delegate. How costly is undoing a wrong call, and how much context does the person bring?

items.prompt: A person new to the company is asked to choose a payroll provider on a multi-year, expensive-to-exit contract. Which level fits best?

Level 4: decide but tell me before acting
items.explanation: Hard to undo plus little context points low. Levels 4 to 6 leave too little room to catch a gap.

items.prompt: What makes a check-in instruction good?
choices: A specific trigger tied to a decision point
A promise to check in sometimes
A daily status message at a set hour
items.explanation: A trigger tied to a decision point leaves both people knowing exactly when the check-in happens.

items.prompt: What is the problem with 'keep me in the loop'?
choices: It asks the delegate to work faster
It forbids the delegate from deciding
It does not say when to check in
items.explanation: Without a time or trigger, the report must guess what looping in means, which recreates the original ambiguity.

items.prompt: In the vendor example, what is the trigger?
choices: Whenever the report feels uncertain
Narrowed to finalists, before signing anything
Every Friday afternoon during the research
items.explanation: The trigger is a decision point, finalists and before signing, which both people can recognize.

items.prompt: What does the example sentence free the delegate from?
choices: Needing approval on which vendors to consider
Reporting any result back at all
Meeting the contract deadline in any form
items.explanation: The manager does not need to approve the small choices, only the final call.

items.prompt: How many check-in moments does the example name?
choices: One per day
One per step
One
items.explanation: The example names a single moment, which is what keeps verification light.

items.prompt: Where should verification concentrate?
choices: On every step in sequence
On one high-leverage moment
On the end, after all work is done
items.explanation: Concentrating on one high-leverage moment protects the decision without reviewing every step.

items.prompt: How does named check-in differ from micromanagement?
choices: It is scoped to one moment, not every step
It asks for more reports than micromanagement
It removes all review from the manager
items.explanation: Micromanagement spreads review over every step; a named check-in is scoped to one moment.

items.prompt: Who must recognize the trigger when it arrives?
choices: Only the manager, who set it
Only the delegate, who does the work
Both the manager and the delegate
items.explanation: A trigger only works if both sides will notice it, which is why it is tied to an event.

items.prompt: A manager asks a report to book a venue. Which check-in line is best?
choices: Keep me posted as the venue search moves along, whenever you can
Pick a shortlist and send it to me before you pay a deposit
Check in with me whenever it makes sense to you
Update me weekly on how the search is going
items.explanation: Only the first names a decision point both can recognize. The rest leave the timing to guesses.

check in: finalists, before signing
no approval needed on small choices
Why: one named trigger moves verification to the moment that matters.

Telling the manager the work existed

items.prompt: How did research quality compare before and after?
choices: It was much better after the change
It was much worse after the change
It was the same in both versions
items.explanation: The research was equally careful in both versions; only the process around it changed.

items.prompt: What changed in the 'after' conversation?
choices: The report did far more research work
One sentence naming the level and trigger
The manager reviewed each daily step
items.explanation: A single added sentence naming Level 3 and the finalists trigger was the only structural change.

items.prompt: A mismatch like this calls for:
choices: A clearer level-setting conversation next time
Moving the report to Level 1 on all tasks
Taking vendor choices away from the report
items.explanation: A mismatch shows the level was unclear, so the repair is to state it more clearly next time.

items.prompt: What did the fix cost?
choices: Weeks of extra reviews
A new tool for tracking tasks
One added sentence
items.explanation: The fix was one sentence in the original request, no extra tools or meetings.

items.prompt: What did the manager's knowledge of Vendor A need?
choices: A formal report from the research team
A moment to arrive before the choice was final
A promise that the report would agree
items.explanation: The manager's context was useful but only if it could arrive while the decision was still reversible.

items.prompt: Was the incident mainly a skill gap?
choices: No; it was a gap in the process
Yes; the report lacked research skill
Yes; the manager lacked management skill
items.explanation: The research was solid; what was missing was a point for the manager to weigh in.

items.prompt: Who benefits from the named trigger?
choices: Only the manager, who gets control
Only the report, who gets freedom
Both the manager and the report
items.explanation: The manager gets the chance to contribute and the report gets a clear limit on their authority.

items.prompt: A report delivers excellent work, but a stakeholder objects because they were never asked. What is the most likely diagnosis?
choices: The report's work quality was weaker than it first seemed to everyone
The stakeholder was oversensitive about being consulted
The process had no moment for the stakeholder to weigh in
The report should have worked at a lower level
items.explanation: Good work plus a surprise points to the process. Quality and level choice are not the clues here.
items.reference:
Same work, different process
before: research, sign, tell
after: research, finalists, manager input, sign
research quality: identical
Why: the missing check-in point, not the report's skill, caused the surprise.
items.learnMore:
Process gap vs. skill gap

When delegation goes wrong, the quick explanation is that the person was not good enough. Often the work was fine and the process had no moment for the manager to contribute.

Common mistake

Responding to a mismatch by lowering the person's autonomy everywhere.
items.reflection: Think of a past surprise at work. Was it a skill problem, or was there simply no point at which the right person could weigh in?

Necessary because the report acted dishonestly
items.explanation: One incident shows the level was unclear, not that the person cannot be trusted on every task.

items.learnMore:
Process gap vs. skill gap

When delegation goes wrong, the quick explanation is that the person was not good enough. Often the work was fine and the process had no moment for the manager to contribute.

Common mistake

Responding to a mismatch by lowering the person's autonomy everywhere.
items.reflection: Think of a past surprise at work. Was it a skill problem, or was there simply no point at which the right person could weigh in?

items.prompt: The level is an assessment of:
choices: Demonstrated context for this kind of decision
The delegate's overall worth to the company
The delegate's years in the organization
items.explanation: A level describes demonstrated context for one kind of decision, not the person as a whole.

items.prompt: What does a strong Level 3 recommendation earn?
choices: Full autonomy on every future task
A lower level on the next task
More autonomy on similar decisions
items.explanation: Strong work on a kind of decision is grounds for more autonomy on similar decisions.

items.prompt: After a mismatch, the next step is to:
choices: Never delegate that kind of task again
Set the level more explicitly next time
Drop the delegate to Level 1 permanently
items.explanation: A mismatch is information that the level needs to be stated more clearly, not a verdict on the person.

items.prompt: A third successful, similar evaluation allows:
choices: Moving up a level, such as toward Level 4
Staying at Level 3 forever by policy
Moving down to Level 2 as a precaution
items.explanation: More demonstrated context with unchanged stakes is real grounds to step up a level.

items.prompt: A much bigger, harder-to-reverse decision should:
choices: Shift the level up to Level 6
Keep the same level as before
Shift the level down the spectrum
items.explanation: Higher stakes make a wrong call costlier, so the level shifts toward closer involvement.

items.prompt: Does naming a level once cover all future tasks?
choices: Yes; the level stays for the whole year
No; each task gets its own read
Yes; changing it damages trust
items.explanation: Each task has its own stakes and context, so each gets its own read.

items.prompt: Is the level a rating of the person overall?
choices: No; it is tied to a kind of decision
Yes; it summarizes who they are
Yes; it is shared across all teams
items.explanation: The level is attached to a kind of decision, not to a person's overall standing.

items.prompt: What moves a level from 3 to 4 on a similar task?
choices: A request from the delegate to be trusted
The passage of time alone
Demonstrated context from earlier work
items.explanation: Earlier work shows context for this kind of decision, which is what moves the level.

items.prompt: A report has run this kind of vendor evaluation three times with no surprises. The next one has the same stakes. What is the best move?
choices: Offer Level 4: decide, but tell me before signing
Stay at Level 3 because every contract needs approval
Offer Level 6 so they never need to report
Drop to Level 2 to rebuild confidence
items.explanation: Context has grown and reversibility has not changed, so one step up fits. Level 6 overshoots.

items.learnMore:
Levels move with evidence

A good recommendation is grounds for more autonomy on similar work. A new kind of decision gets its own read of reversibility and context.

Common mistake

Treating a level as a permanent rating or as a one-time reward.
items.reflection: Where could a person you delegate to move up a level on one kind of task, while staying put on another?
